key_insight: CGMap uses distance-resolved graph learning to turn scattered cancer-related signals into an interpretable ranking of candidate genes. This helps researchers narrow their search and connect computational predictions to practical validation.
problem_solved: Cancer-related signals can be dispersed across biological networks, making it difficult to identify which genes deserve follow-up and explain why they were prioritized.
method: Apply a distance-resolved graph-learning framework to organize dispersed cancer-related signals.
Map those signals into structured gene priorities, narrowing the candidate space.
Provide an interpretable path from candidate-gene hypotheses to practical validation.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, CGMap illustrates how graph learning can support interpretable prioritization in biomedical research. Its focus is on actionable candidate selection rather than predictions alone.
visual_elements: A biological network with distance bands highlighting signals near and far from a candidate gene.
A funnel showing scattered cancer-related signals becoming a shortlist of priority genes.
A ranked gene list with visual links to the signals supporting each priority.
A workflow diagram: graph signals → CGMap → gene priorities → experimental validation.
paper_title: Interpretable distance-resolved graph learning for cancer gene priority screening
paper_authors: Chenhao Wang, Shidong Xu, Li Tang, Gang Luo, Yongchang Zhang
